vignette:
Malia had been a park ranger for nearly fifteen years, her love for the vast, quiet wilderness a stark contrast to the chaotic landscape she had navigated just five years prior as a relief worker. It was during her last deployment that everything changed. She remembered the acrid smell of burning tires, the distant crackle of gunfire, and the constant hum of fear in the air. One afternoon, a sudden explosion had rocked their compound, throwing her against a wall. The next moments were a blur of dust and screams. She had been trying to help a young boy, pulling him towards cover, when a man in a military uniform, reeking of a distinctive, sweet cologne, had roughly pushed past her, his arm brushing her face as he ran. She couldn't recall what happened to the boy, or the man, or even how she got back to safety. When she tried to explain the incident to her colleagues later, or even to her husband, David, she would lose the thread entirely, her words tangling, unable to finish the story. Even to herself, she couldn't tell a clear, coherent narrative of what truly unfolded, though some fragments, like the man’s cologne or the boy’s wide, terrified eyes, remained intensely vivid, while other crucial moments were completely blank.

In the years since returning home, Malia found the tranquility of the redwood forest she patrolled increasingly difficult to appreciate. Her mind was a constant sentinel. Every rustle in the undergrowth, every sudden movement from a hiker on the trail, would immediately put her on guard, her muscles tensing, ready to react to a perceived threat that never materialized. This hypervigilance extended to people as well; she was constantly scrutinizing faces, scanning for any sign of danger, her eyes darting from person to person at the ranger station or in town. She found herself avoiding unfamiliar trails or new sections of the park, explaining to her supervisor that she preferred to stick to routes she knew well, but in truth, it was because she felt she couldn't adequately assess the danger in new, unknown surroundings.

The triggers were relentless. A sudden memory of the explosion would come to mind without warning, flashing behind her eyes even as she drove her patrol vehicle. The specific scent of a certain cologne or perfume, perhaps worn by a tourist or a colleague, would transport her back to that chaotic moment, leaving her breathless and disoriented. Even expressions of affection had become fraught. David’s attempts to hug her often felt like an intrusion, a sudden, unwanted closeness that would make her stiffen, her body bracing for impact, confusing and hurting him. She had come to believe that she had acted in ways that went against who she was during the trauma, a deep-seated conviction that corroded her sense of self. This feeling that she no longer belonged anywhere, that the person she was before the war was gone, led her to withdraw further. She stopped attending the small community church they had always gone to, the close-knit atmosphere feeling too overwhelming, too vulnerable.

Over time, her life narrowed. David noticed her increasing distance, her reluctance to talk about anything beyond the superficial. Her job, once a source of immense joy, now felt like a constant battle against her own internal alarms. She would often cut patrols short, or avoid areas where she knew she might encounter more people. The thought of seeking medical or psychological help felt like an admission of profound weakness, a confirmation of her deepest fear that her life was not worth living anymore, that she was irreparably broken. It was only when her supervisor expressed concern about her performance, subtly suggesting she take some time off, that Malia finally conceded. The thought of losing the one stable anchor she had left, her job, pushed her to make the first difficult call, her voice trembling as she scheduled an appointment, still terrified of what she might uncover, but even more afraid of continuing to live this way.
